item.title: Two Roads to Competence? How Cognitive and Affective Individual Differences Reach Applied Performance by Different Routes
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Individual differences predict applied competence, but the routes by which they do so are rarely modelled. Drawing on investment and aptitude theory for cognitive resources and on appraisal theory for affective orientations, we propose an appraisal-correspondence principle: the closer an individual-difference variable stands to the outcome in its level of self-appraisal, the more directly it should act; the further away it is, the more mediation should be required. We tested the principle on pre-service teachers’ competence to teach with generative artificial intelligence (AI-TPACK), using a latent-variable model on cross-sectional data from 164 pre-service primary-school teachers in Türkiye. AI readiness (cognitive) and AI competence anxiety (affective) served as antecedents and generative AI literacy and AI self-efficacy as mediators. Fit was good, χ2(139) = 181.44, CFI = 0.978, TLI = 0.973, RMSEA = 0.045, and SRMR = 0.061, with 45.8% of AI-TPACK variance explained. Readiness produced a strong total effect (β = 0.600, 95% CI [0.444, 0.738]), half of it indirect; model comparison indicated that generative AI literacy, rather than self-efficacy, carries the mediated share, although the literacy → AI-TPACK path itself was only partially supported. Competence anxiety predicted neither mediator, and its direct path to AI-TPACK was small (β = −0.105, CI [−0.266, 0.059]) and not significant in any of 16 pre-specified data-handling variants. The cognitive road is robust; the affective road, as predicted by the principle, bypasses the mediators but leaves only a faint and uncertain trace. Full scalar invariance held across year of study and use frequency. We state the principle as a hypothesis for performance-based tests rather than as an established mechanism.

item.title: Assessing learning beyond AI assistance: assisted performance and unaided retention in generative AI-supported learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve task performance when support is available, yet these gains do not necessarily indicate what learners retain independently. This Mini Review examines three assessment conditions: assisted task performance, immediate testing without AI, and delayed testing without AI. Relevant evidence was identified through searches of the Web of Science Core Collection and supplementary source identification. Across the reviewed experiments, outcomes varied with task demands, instructional design and the skills assessed. Unrestricted AI assistance was associated with weaker subsequent performance in some comparisons, whereas structured AI-supported instruction showed benefits for selected outcomes. None of the twelve selected studies documented all three conditions with verified AI exclusion at both no-AI posttests. Variation in baseline measurement, follow-up intervals and instructional comparators further limits cross-study interpretation. Retrieval attempts, elaboration and feedback use offer plausible explanations, but their roles as mediators remain largely untested. Future studies should document AI availability during learning and testing, specify the constructs assessed, and report learning activities between assessments.

item.title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

item.title: Generative AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement in university EFL writing: a mixed-methods study of autonomy, self-regulated learning, and AI literacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

item.title: Effects of structured generative AI feedback on data science students' critical thinking: a propensity score matching approach
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course ( N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p < 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

item.title: From emotional comfort to relational investment in generative AI companionship: evidence from SEM and fsQCA
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
With the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI), chatbots are evolving from instrumental assistants into emotionally responsive companions. This study develops a low-friction relational process model to examine the relationships linking generative AI companionship with emotional relief and positive social investment. AI emotional responsiveness, non-judgemental interaction, and memory-based continuity were conceptualized as interaction conditions, while perceived being understood, deep self-disclosure, and synthetic attachment were specified as psychological mechanisms. Structural equation modeling (SEM), bootstrap mediation analysis, moderation analysis, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were employed to analyse 765 valid responses from generative AI chatbot users. The SEM results show that non-judgemental interaction exhibits the most consistent pattern of associations with perceived being understood, deep self-disclosure, synthetic attachment, emotional relief, and positive social investment. Perceived being understood and synthetic attachment show relatively stable mediating patterns, whereas deep self-disclosure is significantly associated with emotional relief but shows a less consistent association with positive social investment. Perceived AI safety and self-disclosure habit play differentiated moderating roles. The fsQCA findings reveal three configurations for high emotional relief and four configurations for high positive social investment, complementing the SEM results. This study provides a systematic account of generative AI companionship and offers implications for safer and relationship-oriented AI design.

item.title: Exploring attentional bias in posttraumatic stress disorder: insights from police officers with service dogs
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction PTSD is characterized by hypervigilance and attentional bias to threat, which can severely interfere with daily functioning. Stress exacerbates this bias by increasing amygdala activity and depleting prefrontal resources, reducing attentional control. The presence of a dog may help regulate attention by reducing stress. Methods This study investigates attentional bias to emotional faces in police officers with PTSD and examines whether the presence of their service or companion dog diminishes this bias by mitigating stress-related cognitive depletion, using a within subject design. Police officers with ( n = 24) and without PTSD ( n = 24) completed the dot-probe task with angry and happy faces in the presence and absence of their dog. Reaction times and event-related potentials (ERP) were analyzed to assess attentional bias. Results Officers with PTSD showed a greater trial level bias score but no consistent bias direction. The P3 amplitude indicated no differentiation between happy and angry faces in the PTSD group, unlike the control group. The VPP amplitude was higher in the PTSD group when the dog was absent, suggesting increased early-stage attention to faces without the dog. Officers with PTSD showed also slower reaction times when their dog was absent. Discussion The findings suggest that PTSD is associated with a reduced ability to selectively allocate attention based on emotional content and increased reaction time variability rather than a consistent directional bias toward or away from emotional stimuli. The presence of a dog appeared to regulate early-stage attentional processing and reaction speed.

item.title: An EMG-driven virtual reality platform for physiology-based motor interaction: technical and functional validation
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Harnessing experience-dependent neuroplasticity has become a central goal of modern neurorehabilitation. Immersive virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool, enabling task-oriented training in ecologically valid scenarios that are difficult to reproduce in conventional clinical settings. Despite these advances, interaction in most existing VR rehabilitation systems remains primarily mediated by external interfaces, such as motion tracking or handheld controllers, rather than by the user’s own physiological motor activity. Consequently, rehabilitation often fails to directly engage the physiological motor commands that naturally drive voluntary movement. We present and validate an integrated VR–electromyography (VR-EMG) platform that enables closed-loop, physiology-driven interaction between users and immersive virtual environments. The platform combines a standalone VR architecture with wearable EMG systems, online EMG decoding, and cloud-based performance monitoring within a unified framework. A standardized motor-command interface enables different EMG acquisition systems to control both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic virtual effectors without modifying the decoding strategy or rehabilitation scenarios, providing a flexible framework for diverse applications. The platform was validated through complementary technical and functional evaluations performed on the two supported EMG acquisition systems. Technical validation assessed signal quality, gesture classification accuracy, communication latency, and system reliability. Functional validation was conducted in individuals with upper-limb amputation and able-bodied controls while performing object-interaction tasks across multiple immersive virtual scenarios. The platform demonstrated stable closed-loop operation, reliable gesture recognition, and the ability to quantify objective performance metrics, including task score, completion time, gesture classification errors, precision errors, correctly recognized gestures, and user-reported workload. Findings demonstrate the feasibility, technical reliability, and functional versatility of the proposed platform by providing a physiology-driven framework for immersive motor interaction that is compatible with different EMG acquisition systems and dissociates motor control from the morphology of the controlled virtual effector. Because the two systems were used for different components of the validation, we do not establish equivalence in their performance. By integrating online EMG decoding, VR, and quantitative performance monitoring, the platform offers a tool for future applications in rehabilitation, prosthetic training, and studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging and high-density electroencephalography to address whether training with the platform induces changes in functional brain organization.

item.title: When AI Shows Its Rationale: User-Visible Rationale Styles and the Adoption of AI-Mediated Relational Correction
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

item.title: Generative operationalism: when LLM-based item generation displaces construct theory in educational and psychological measurement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly changing automated item generation (AIG) by enabling researchers to produce extensive pools of educational and psychological items with little time and human labor. Although this development is usually discussed as a technical improvement in test construction, it raises a more fundamental philosophical question: What warrants the claim that a machine-generated item measures the attribute assigned to it? This paper introduces the concept of generative operationalism to describe a mode of test development in which an ordinary-language construct label is supplied to a generative model, its outputs are treated as operationalizations of that construct, and post-hoc psychometric regularities are subsequently interpreted as evidence that the construct has been successfully measured. Drawing primarily on causal realism, we argue that LLM-generated items are not necessarily invalid for measuring their target attributes, but rather, theory-displacing uses of AIG weaken the epistemic warrant for the proposed causal pathway from the target attribute to the observed response. They may also produce semantic redundancy, construct underrepresentation, method variance, and residual dependence that generate apparently desirable psychometric properties without establishing that the intended attribute causally influences responses. The central problem is therefore not machine authorship itself, but the substitution of linguistic plausibility and statistical regularity for an independently articulated theory of the construct and its response processes. We conclude by specifying conditions under which LLMs can function as theory-implementing instruments rather than engines of generative operationalism .

item.title: From cognitive relief to motivational enhancement: associations between perceived Agentic AI Capability and student engagement in systems development courses
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

item.title: Human–machine collaborative literacy and tourism SMEs’ perceived digital transformation performance: a configurational fsQCA
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in tourism service work, employees increasingly need to interpret machine-generated outputs, evaluate their usefulness, and integrate them into organisational activities. Yet little is known about the firm-level resource configurations in which workforce human–machine collaborative literacy (HC) accompanies favourable digital transformation performance. Integrating organisational psychology perspectives on human–AI work with the technology–organisation–environment framework and a digital eco-embedding perspective, this study applied fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to 401 managerial questionnaires aggregated to 30 Chinese tourism small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The analysis examined manager-perceived workforce HC alongside intelligent technology infrastructure (TI), digital niche (IO), policy support (PS), and open innovation networks (CN). No individual condition or its negation was necessary for high perceived performance (HC necessity consistency = 0.845). Two high-performance configurations shared core TI and IO: H1 included peripheral CN, with HC unspecified, whereas H2 included peripheral HC and PS. Seven firms satisfied the descriptive membership criterion for both high-performance configurations. Three non-high-performance configurations shared the absence of digital niche (~IO), with the absence of HC specified in two. The intermediate expressions were retained across the examined calibration and truth-table threshold settings. In the leave-one-firm-out analyses, the complete high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 28 of 30 deletions and the H2 conjunction in all 30, whereas the complete non-high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 20 of 30 deletions. These findings position manager-perceived workforce HC as a configuration-specific complement rather than a universally necessary condition for favourable perceived transformation performance. By situating a workforce-related capability within technological, ecosystem, and institutional resource configurations, the study provides an organisational-level contextual perspective on human–AI collaboration. The findings suggest that workforce capability development should be considered alongside technological readiness, digital ecosystem access, and institutional support.

item.title: When does AI assistance undermine relational authenticity? A mini review of conditional effects in AI-mediated interpersonal communication
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Research on AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) has produced seemingly contradictory findings on how AI assistance affects interpersonal relationships. Disclosed use lowers trust, behavioral measures show null effects, and under realistic conditions receivers do not suspect use at all. This mini review integrates experimental studies conducted in interpersonal contexts and argues that these conflicting findings may be reconciled by a conditional-effects framework. Thirteen core experimental studies and four auxiliary studies from adjacent domains, identified through multi-database searches, were coded on four moderators and on the mediators they tested. Relational costs concentrate under four conditions: disclosure or suspicion of use, message emotionality, relational closeness, and level of assistance. Because the moderators are confounded across studies, the framework is offered as an organizing structure rather than a settled resolution; within-study evidence supports the moderators to differing degrees, with level of assistance the most consistently supported and relational closeness the least. Diminished perceived authorship, comprising a cognitive attribution component and a relational-obligation component, is proposed as a candidate mechanism; it is indirectly supported by the mediators tested to date but has not been tested directly. The review states falsifiable propositions for each moderator, flags anomalous findings, notes measurement problems, and outlines priorities for longitudinal, psychometric, and cross-cultural research.

item.title: Artificial intelligence readiness and innovative work behavior among university engineering teachers: parallel indirect effects of creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of university teachers’ teaching and research, yet its relationship with innovative work behavior in engineering education remains unclear. Methods Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory, this cross-sectional study surveyed 786 university engineering teachers in Chongqing, China. We examined the association between AI readiness and innovative work behavior and tested parallel indirect effects through creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy. Gender and educational attainment were included as covariates. Results AI readiness was positively associated with innovative work behavior. The indirect paths through creative self-efficacy and technology integration self-efficacy were both significant. AI readiness remained significantly associated with innovative work behavior after both mediators were included, indicating partial mediation. Discussion These findings suggest that AI readiness and efficacy beliefs may support innovative work among engineering teachers. Universities can support quality education by linking AI training to course design, laboratory teaching, project development, and research tasks, while using guided practice and feedback to build teachers’ confidence.

item.title: Teaching while researching in a smart classroom: community-engaged action research on microlecturing for teachers’ professional learning
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract The widespread digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, have largely elevated student experiences and achievements in higher education, but the simultaneous upgrade of teacher capacity, particularly the resources and opportunities for teachers’ professional development in everyday class, were less attended. To investigate how a smart classroom can be orchestrated to boost teachers’ self-exploration and collaboration in digital teaching, this study employed the technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) framework to probe how teachers advanced their professional learning through design, implementation, and revision of VoiceThread microlectures for students’ Chinese character learning outside the class. Collaborative action research was conducted over four years to create a teaching community comprising the researcher and five teachers to enhance contextual smartness, that is, digital technologies and teachers’ context-aware, adaptive, and personalized use of them, in Chinese language classrooms. Semi-structured teacher interviews, community discussion, and surveys from 227 students showed that teachers utilized microlecturing to strengthen their TPACK about Chinese characters alongside class progress. This TPACKing process not just promoted research-practice dialogues but reinforced teachers’ beliefs and strategies to carry out professional learning in smart classrooms. The findings suggested a dynamic re-framing of TPACK with means of updating and interacting with contexts, content, technologies, and pedagogies in smart learning environments. The study also offered tips to keep up language teachers’ continuing professional development in daily instruction.

item.title: Perceived weight status, body image, and depressive symptoms in Korean adolescents: a three-wave longitudinal study and within-person analysis
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Body dissatisfaction is a well-established risk factor for adolescent depression, but two questions remain open. First, it is unclear whether perceived weight status—a subjective cognitive appraisal of one’s body—relates to body image and depression differently from objective body size. Second, most longitudinal evidence relies on between-person models that cannot isolate within-person change. Drawing on a cognitive-behavioral model of body image, we distinguish perceived weight status (a perceptual-categorical appraisal) from body image (the attitudinal-evaluative dimension) and examine both between- and within-person processes. We analyzed three-wave longitudinal data from the Panel Study on Korean Children (ages 13–15; analytic N = 1,148–1,304). A temporally ordered mediation model (perceived weight status at Wave 14 → body image at Wave 15 → depressive symptoms at Wave 16) was estimated using structural equation modeling, controlling for prior depressive symptoms and sex-standardized BMI. Indirect effects were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap resamples with bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals. We examined within-person dynamics using two- and three-variable random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs). Body image was assessed using a refined 4-item scale (α = .735, ω = .77). Perceiving oneself as heavier at W14 predicted a less positive body image at W15 (β = −0.126, p < .001), which in turn predicted higher depressive symptoms at W16 (β = −0.101, p < .001), yielding a small but significant indirect effect (0.013, 95% BCa CI [0.005, 0.025]). Sex-standardized BMI did not significantly predict body image (β = −0.064, p = .091), but the coefficients for perceived weight status and BMI did not differ significantly (Δ = −0.062, p = .368). The indirect effect did not differ by sex (Δ = −0.003, p = .776), although the component paths did. In the RI-CLPM, perceived weight status showed no prospective within-person association with body image ( p = .135) or depressive symptoms ( p = .594). In contrast, body image and depressive symptoms were reciprocally associated within persons (both ps < .01), independent of stable between-person differences. Perceived weight status was prospectively associated with body image, while body image and depressive symptoms showed reciprocal within-person associations. However, the mediational pathway was not supported at the within-person level, suggesting that the observed indirect association may primarily reflect between-person differences. Prevention and intervention efforts may therefore benefit from targeting the reciprocal body image–depression cycle rather than assuming a unidirectional, perception-driven pathway.

item.title: Emotions and anthropomorphism towards robots: a scoping review
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Human interaction with non-human entities, such as robots, has long been characterised by anthropomorphism – namely, the tendency to attribute human-like mental states to inanimate objects. While humans appear evolutionarily hardwired to use anthropomorphism as the default strategy for navigating interactions with their peers, significant gaps remain in the Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) field in defining and operationalising “emotions” and their relationship to psychological anthropomorphism towards robots. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing HRI literature and see how emotions are investigated in relation to robots. By reviewing relevant empirical studies, it addresses four core research questions focusing on: (i) the conceptualisation of emotions and anthropomorphism towards robots; (ii) prevailing theoretical models and definitions; (iii) methodologies used to investigate emotions in HRI; and (iv) key findings in the literature regarding the emotions-anthropomorphism link. This review contributes to broaden current discussions about how emotions are conceptualised and analysed in HRI research, by which it would be possible to contribute to extend knowledge about how people emotionally interact with robots by considering their anthropomorphism.
